short_title: Disease Vector Control and Ship Health Certificates
text_verbatim: Control of disease vectors is necessary for maintenance of health on board ships. What is the Role the WHO organisation in this regard and which are the national agencies tasked with this maintenance of the ship and the crew in good health? What are the different certificates issued to a vessel for maintenance of the ship in good health? Who can issue these certificates in India and what is the validity and extension options? (16)

blocks.p: Ship health and vector control are governed by the International Health Regulations (2005), a binding instrument of the World Health Organization, as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024. The 2024 amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025. The IHR work through designated points of entry, competent authorities at those points, and a small set of ship documents.

ul: It makes the rules. WHO adopts the IHR and prescribes the model certificates in Annex 3 and the Ship Declaration of Health in Annex 8, so the documents are the same worldwide.

It identifies where vector control is needed. Under Annex 5, WHO publishes on a regular basis a list of areas where disinsection or other vector control measures are recommended for conveyances arriving from them, through temporary or standing recommendations.

It advises methods and materials. Where WHO has advised methods for disinsection, deratting, disinfection or decontamination, those should be used unless the competent authority is satisfied that others are as safe and reliable (Article 27), and States should accept measures applied elsewhere by WHO-advised methods.

It certifies and publishes. On a State Party's request WHO may, after appropriate investigation, certify that a port meets the IHR requirements (Article 20(4)), publishes certification guidelines and the list of certified ports (20(5)), and publishes the lists of authorized ports notified by States Parties (20(3)).

It provides technical guidance - notably the WHO Handbook for inspection of ships and issuance of ship sanitation certificates - and declares Public Health Emergencies of International Concern with temporary recommendations.
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare - the health authority for IHR purposes, under which the National IHR Focal Point sits.

Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), and under it the Port Health Organisation, headed by the Port Health Officer - the competent authority at the point of entry. It inspects ships, baggage, cargo and containers, supervises control measures and issues the ship sanitation certificates, working under the Indian Port Health Rules, 1955 with the IHR 2005.
Directorate General of Shipping, through its Maritime Health Branch, on the seafarer side - approving medical examiners and governing seafarers' medical fitness examination and certification.
Port authorities and the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways support these functions at the ports themselves.

Ship Sanitation Control Exemption Certificate (SSCEC) - issued where the competent authority is satisfied that the ship is free of infection and contamination, including vectors and reservoirs, so that no control measures are required (Article 39(6)).

Ship Sanitation Control Certificate (SSCC) - issued where control measures were required and have been satisfactorily completed, and it records the evidence found and the measures taken (Article 39(5)). Under Annex 5 the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them are recorded on this certificate. If a satisfactory result could not be obtained, the authority notes that on the certificate (Article 39(7)).

blocks.p: Both follow the model in Annex 3, and they replaced the former Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates. Alongside them the master submits a Ship Declaration of Health under Article 37, to the model in Annex 8 - a declaration, not a certificate. Separately, and concerning the crew rather than the ship, seafarers hold medical fitness certificates under MLC 2006 and STCW.

blocks.h: 5. Who issues them in India, validity and extension

ul: In India they are issued by the Port Health Officer at a port authorized for the purpose and notified to WHO. Under Article 20(3) a State Party notifies which ports may issue the SSCC, which may issue the SSCEC only, and which may grant the one-month extension.
Validity: a maximum of six months, for both the SSCEC and the SSCC (Article 39(1)).
Extension: by one month, where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at that port - the extension carries the ship to a port where the certificate can be obtained.

Where no valid certificate is produced, or evidence of a public health risk is found on board, the State Party may proceed under Article 27(1) - treating the ship as affected and requiring disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Control measures are to be carried out whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading (Article 39(4)).

For Indian coastal trade calling where no Port Health Officer is available, DG Shipping has provided for a Statement of Compliance issued by an authorized medical examiner, to be endorsed at the earliest available opportunity.

blocks.p: So the answer to "validity and extension options" on this paper is one pair of numbers, not two: six months, extendable by one month, issued by the Port Health Officer at an authorized port under the IHR. The stem confines the certificate limb to those issued to a vessel, so the seafarer's own medical certificate - which has its own authority, its own validity and its own extension rule under MLC 2006 Standard A1.2 - is outside what is asked here, even though the opening sentence names the crew. Naming the crew's certificate in one line to show you know the boundary costs nothing; answering it at length spends marks the examiner has not offered.

Three questions are asked and each must be visibly answered - WHO's role, the national agencies, and the certificates in India with their validity and extension. Take them in the printed order and head each one. The last limb carries the numbers the examiner is certainly looking for, so never let it be squeezed by a long essay on WHO. Note what this stem does not say: it asks for the certificates "in India", without the qualifier "issued to a vessel for maintenance of the ship in good health" that other sittings of this question print - and its own first sentence names "the ship and the crew". Read plainly, the crew's medical certificate is inside the task. Answer the ship's certificates first and fully, then give the crew's its own short paragraph. That way you are complete on the wider reading and lose nothing on the narrower one.

blocks.h: The currency point that will separate answers

blocks.p: The IHR were amended in 2024 and those amendments entered into force on 19 September 2025 - just two months before this paper was sat. One visible consequence: Article 37 is now the "Ship Declaration of Health". In the original 2005 text it was the "Maritime Declaration of Health", and that older name is what almost every textbook, coaching note and older syllabus still uses. Both texts were compared directly for this answer: the original uses "Maritime Declaration of Health" throughout and never the new name; the consolidated amended text uses "Ship Declaration of Health" throughout and never the old one. Using the current name, and being able to say why it changed, is a cheap and genuine mark.

blocks.h: Ship health and crew health are two different systems

blocks.p: The question asks about "the ship and the crew", and the two run on separate tracks with separate authorities. Ship health is WHO and the IHR, administered in India by the Port Health Organisation under DGHS and the Ministry of Health, and evidenced by the SSCC or SSCEC. Crew health is MLC 2006 and STCW, administered in India by DG Shipping through approved medical examiners, and evidenced by seafarers' medical fitness certificates. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates. It is not - the Port Health Officer issues those.

ul: Calling the SSCC/SSCEC a Deratting Certificate. Those were the predecessors under the earlier Regulations and were replaced under the IHR 2005 - the scope widened from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.
Saying the certificates are valid for six months extendable by six months. The extension is one month, and only where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at that port.
Confusing the SSCC with the SSCEC. Exemption means no measures were needed; Control means measures were required and were completed.
Treating the Ship Declaration of Health as a certificate. It is a declaration by the master, to the Annex 8 model, and a State may dispense with it entirely under Article 37(4).
Naming WHO as an enforcement body. WHO recommends, certifies ports on request and publishes; the competent authority at the point of entry enforces.

blocks.p:
"Your certificate expired yesterday and the port cannot inspect - what happens?" The one-month extension in Article 39(1) exists precisely for this, and under Article 20(3)(c) States notify which of their ports may grant it, so that the ship can reach a port where the certificate is obtainable.

"When should the inspection be done?" Whenever possible with the ship and holds empty, and for a ship in ballast before loading - Article 39(4). Answering "any time" misses a printed requirement.

"What does WHO actually do about mosquitoes?" It publishes the list of areas where vector control is recommended for conveyances arriving from them, and advises the methods. States Parties then run vector control programmes at points of entry - to a minimum distance of 400 metres from the operational areas under Annex 5.

ul: Who issues the SSCC in India? The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO.
Under which ministry does the Port Health Organisation sit? The Directorate General of Health Services, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Validity and extension? Maximum six months; extendable by one month where the inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at the port.
What is recorded on an SSCC? The evidence found and the control measures taken - including, under Annex 5, the presence of vectors on board and the measures used to eradicate them.
What happens if you cannot produce a valid certificate? The State Party may treat the ship as affected under Article 27(1) and require disinfection, decontamination, disinsection or deratting.
Which convention covers the crew's medical fitness rather than the ship's sanitation? MLC 2006, with STCW for certification - administered in India by DG Shipping.

blocks.p: RULE - AGENCY - PAPER - TWO CLOCKS. Rule: IHR 2005 as amended, WHO's role (steps 1 to 2). Agency: MoHFW, DGHS, Port Health Organisation and the Port Health Officer, with DG Shipping on the crew side (step 3). Paper: SSCEC, SSCC and the Ship Declaration of Health (step 4). Two clocks, and this is the part that answers the printed words 'validity and extension options': the ship runs on six months plus one (step 5); the crew runs on two years plus three months (step 6). Same idea, different numbers, different authority.

ul: International Health Regulations (2005), as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024; the 2024 amendments in force 19 September 2025

IHR Article 20(3) - States notify WHO of ports authorized to issue the SSCC, to issue the SSCEC only, and to grant the one-month extension; Article 20(4)-(5) - WHO certification of ports and certification guidelines
IHR Article 22 - role of competent authorities at points of entry
IHR Article 24(1)(c) - conveyance operators to keep conveyances free of sources of infection and contamination, including vectors and reservoirs
IHR Article 27(1) - affected conveyances: disinfect, decontaminate, disinsect or derat
IHR Article 37 - Ship Declaration of Health, model in Annex 8 (titled Maritime Declaration of Health in the original 2005 text)

IHR Article 39 - ship sanitation certificates: 39(1) six months, extendable by one month; 39(3) model in Annex 3; 39(4) ship and holds empty, in ballast before loading; 39(5) SSCC on completion of measures; 39(6) SSCEC where free of infection and contamination; 39(7) note where a satisfactory result cannot be obtained
IHR Annex 3 - model ship sanitation certificates; Annex 8 - model Ship Declaration of Health
IHR Annex 5 - vector-borne diseases: WHO list of areas, recording of vectors on the SSCC, and vector control programmes to a minimum of 400 metres from point of entry operational areas
Indian Port Health Rules, 1955, read with the IHR 2005; DG Shipping Order 10 of 2018 (revised) for the Statement of Compliance route

blocks.p: The IHR content in this answer is primary-verified, read in the consolidated WHO text as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024, and the renaming of the Declaration of Health was confirmed by reading the original 2005 text alongside it rather than by inference. Two areas are weaker. The Indian administrative detail - the position of the Port Health Organisation under DGHS, the Indian Port Health Rules 1955, and the DG Shipping Statement of Compliance route for coastal trade - rests on Government and classification-society restatements rather than on the order and rules texts themselves, and is stated at that level of confidence. The list of authorized Indian ports is deliberately not reproduced: it is notified by the State Party to WHO and changes, so naming ports in a study answer would date badly. A candidate asked for specifics should say that the list is notified to and published by WHO rather than guess at it.

blocks.h: Two clocks, and why the examiner set the word "options"

blocks.p: The printed words are "validity and extension options" - plural. On this stem that plural has a real answer, because two different certificate regimes are in play and each has its own pair of numbers. The ship runs on the IHR: six months, extended by one month, and the extension exists so that a ship can reach a port where the inspection can actually be done. The crew runs on MLC Standard A1.2: two years (one if under 18, six for colour vision), extended by up to three months to the next port of call where a practitioner is available. Notice that the two extensions are built on the same idea - the document expires while the ship is somewhere the issuer is not - and that neither is a favour: both are capped, and both run to the next place the thing can be done properly. If you can set those two side by side in three lines you have answered the last limb completely, and very few candidates will.

blocks.h: Do not put DG Shipping in charge of the ship

blocks.p: This is the error that costs most marks on the India limb, and the widened certificate limb on this paper makes it easier to fall into, because both authorities now appear in the same answer. Keep them apart: the Port Health Officer, under the Port Health Organisation, DGHS and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, certifies the ship - SSCC and SSCEC, under the IHR and the Indian Port Health Rules 1955. DG Shipping, under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, approves the medical examiners who certify the seafarer. Health ministry for the hull; shipping administration for the man. Write that sentence and the limb is safe.

blocks.h: What this sitting does NOT ask, and why that is worth knowing

blocks.p: The November 2025 paper set this question in a shorter form - it asked for "the different certificates in India" with no qualifier. That omission widened the task: with nothing confining the certificates to the ship, and with the opening sentence naming the ship and the crew, the seafarer's medical certificate under MLC 2006 Regulation 1.2 and Standard A1.2 fell inside the printed demand and had to be answered - two years' validity, one year under 18, six years for colour vision, and a certificate expiring at sea continuing to the next port for not more than three months. This paper puts the qualifier back: certificates issued to a vessel for maintenance of the ship in good health. That single phrase moves the crew's certificate out of the task. Learn both, because the two sittings are one month apart and the difference between them is a phrase rather than a topic - and the skill being tested is reading the stem, not reciting the subject. The safe technique is a single sentence acknowledging that the crew hold their own certificate under a different instrument and a different authority, then spending the marks where the stem points.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: An institutional and certification question: who sets the rules, who administers them in India, what documents result, and how long they last. Vector control is the entry point rather than the whole subject. On THIS stem the certificate limb is not confined to the ship, so it runs across both the ship-health and crew-health systems.

quick_revision.recall_15s: IHR 2005 as amended 2014, 2022 and 2024 - the 2024 amendments in force 19 September 2025. WHO: makes the rules and the Annex 3 and Annex 8 models; publishes the list of areas where vector control is recommended (Annex 5); advises methods; certifies ports on request (Art 20(4)) and publishes authorized-port lists (Art 20(3)); issues the inspection Handbook. India: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, DGHS, and the Port Health Organisation under it - the Port Health Officer is the competent authority and issues the certificates under the Indian Port Health Rules 1955 with the IHR; DG Shipping handles seafarer medical fitness. Certificates: SSCEC where no measures needed (Art 39(6)); SSCC where measures were required and completed, recording evidence and measures (Art 39(5)) - both to the Annex 3 model, replacing the old Deratting certificates. Plus the master's Ship Declaration of Health under Art 37 to the Annex 8 model. Validity SIX MONTHS, extendable by ONE MONTH where inspection or measures cannot be accomplished at the port (Art 39(1)).
critical_numbers: Ship sanitation certificates valid a maximum of six months (Art 39(1))
Extendable by one month where inspection or control measures cannot be accomplished at the port
2024 IHR amendments entered into force 19 September 2025
Vector control programmes to a minimum of 400 metres from point of entry operational areas (Annex 5)
quick_revision.critical_regulation: IHR (2005) Article 39 - ship sanitation certificates, maximum six months and extendable by one month; models in Annex 3
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying the extension is six months rather than one month, and still calling the document a Deratting Certificate. Note also that under the amendments in force since 19 September 2025 Article 37 is the Ship Declaration of Health, not the Maritime Declaration of Health. The scope trap at this sitting is the opposite of a gap: the stem asks for certificates issued to a vessel, so a long answer on the seafarer's medical certificate earns nothing here.

Art 20(3) - ports notified for issue, exemption only, or extension
valid a maximum of six months
extendable by one month where measures cannot be accomplished at the port
no valid certificate or risk found - Art 27(1) applies
measures when ship and holds empty; in ballast before loading
Statement of Compliance route for Indian coastal trade

understand_first: There are two health systems on a ship and the question runs across both. One protects the world from the ship - vectors, infection and contamination crossing borders in a hull - and that is WHO's International Health Regulations, enforced by a port health authority and evidenced by a ship sanitation certificate. The other protects the crew, and that is labour and training law administered by the shipping administration. Keeping those two apart is what makes the India limb straightforward: the Port Health Officer certifies the ship, DG Shipping certifies the seafarer.
memory_cue: RULE (steps 1-2) - AGENCY (3) - PAPER (4) - ONE CLOCK (5): six months plus one, from the Port Health Officer. Four printed demands, so do not let the framework crowd out the fourth: who issues is asked separately at this sitting and carries its own marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the ship health and WHO question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The governing instrument. 2 The role of WHO. 3 National agencies in India. 4 The ship's certificates. 5 Issue in India, validity and extension for the ship. 6 The crew's medical certificate, its validity and its own extension.
retrieval_cards.why: Follows the three printed tasks in order, with the framework first - and splits the certificate limb between ship and crew, because this stem asks for the certificates 'in India' without confining them to the ship.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long are ship sanitation certificates valid, and what extension is available?
retrieval_cards.answer: A maximum of six months, for both the SSCC and the SSCEC. Extendable by one month where the inspection or the required control measures cannot be accomplished at the port. IHR Article 39(1).
retrieval_cards.why: The single most examined fact in this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the SSCC from the SSCEC.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Exemption Certificate is issued where the authority is satisfied the ship is free of infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs, so no measures are needed. The Control Certificate is issued where measures were required and satisfactorily completed, and records the evidence found and the measures taken.
retrieval_cards.why: Exemption means nothing was needed; Control means something was done.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is Article 37 called now, and what was it called before?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Ship Declaration of Health, to the model in Annex 8. In the original 2005 text it was the Maritime Declaration of Health. The change came with the amendments in force from 19 September 2025.
retrieval_cards.why: Most textbooks and coaching notes still use the old name.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are these still called Deratting Certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Deratting and Deratting Exemption Certificates of the earlier Regulations were replaced under the IHR 2005 by the SSCC and SSCEC, widening the scope from rodents to all infection and contamination including vectors and reservoirs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who issues ship sanitation certificates in India?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Port Health Officer, at a port authorized for the purpose and notified by India to WHO. The Port Health Organisation sits under the Directorate General of Health Services, within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and works under the Indian Port Health Rules 1955 with the IHR 2005.
retrieval_cards.why: Not DG Shipping - that side handles seafarer medical fitness.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Summarise WHO's role in four verbs.
retrieval_cards.answer: It prescribes (the Regulations and the Annex 3 and 8 models), publishes (areas where vector control is recommended, and lists of authorized ports), advises (methods and materials for disinsection and deratting) and certifies (ports, on the State Party's request, under Article 20(4)).
retrieval_cards.why: WHO does not enforce - the competent authority at the point of entry does.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What distance does Annex 5 set for vector control programmes at points of entry?
retrieval_cards.answer: A minimum of 400 metres from those areas of point of entry facilities used for operations involving travellers, conveyances, containers, cargo and postal parcels - extended where vectors of greater range are present.
retrieval_cards.why: A precise, checkable figure that shows the Annex has been read.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When should the sanitation inspection be carried out?
retrieval_cards.answer: Whenever possible when the ship and holds are empty, and in the case of a ship in ballast, before loading. IHR Article 39(4).
retrieval_cards.why: A printed requirement candidates routinely miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: No valid certificate is produced on arrival - what may the State Party do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Proceed under Article 27(1): treat the conveyance as affected and disinfect, decontaminate, disinsect or derat it, or have that done under its supervision, with isolation or quarantine if necessary.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian authority certifies the ship's health, and which certifies the seafarer's?
retrieval_cards.answer: The ship: the Port Health Officer, in the Port Health Organisation under the Directorate General of Health Services and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, issuing the SSCC or SSCEC under the IHR 2005 and the Indian Port Health Rules 1955. The seafarer: a medical examiner approved by the Directorate General of Shipping, which acts under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, issuing the medical fitness certificate under MLC 2006 Standard A1.2 and STCW.
retrieval_cards.why: Health ministry for the hull, shipping administration for the man. Candidates routinely put DG Shipping in charge of ship sanitation certificates.

notes: FORWARD DONOR, ONE MONTH. The governing amendment - the 2024 amendments to the IHR (2005) - entered into force on 19 September 2025, which is before BOTH sittings. The donor's currency point therefore carries forward rather than reversing, and the only figure that moves is the interval: about two and a half months here against two for the donor. Article 37 is the Ship Declaration of Health at this sitting, not the Maritime Declaration of Health.

CURRENCY RE-CHECK OVER THE ONE-MONTH GAP. The donor's B_CURRENCY_CHECK asked whether any further IHR amendment entered into force between 19 September 2025 and the November sitting; none had. The same question was asked again for the additional month to December 2025 and the answer is the same. The check is recorded rather than inherited.

THE 34TH ASSEMBLY BOUNDARY IS CHECKED AND NOT ENGAGED. QP2512 excludes the whole A.12xx(34) family - see QP2512_TEMPORAL_AND_DONOR_ANCHOR.md. This answer rests on a World Health Assembly instrument, on Indian subordinate legislation and on MLC provisions in the study layer only. No IMO Assembly resolution of any session is cited. Negative finding, recorded.

THE MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT BOUNDARY IS ENGAGED ONLY IN THE AGENCIES LIMB, AND CORRECTLY. DG Shipping acts under the MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT 1958, which is the operative Indian statute at this sitting - the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had assent from 18 August 2025 but did not commence until 15 March 2026. The donor already states the 1958 Act and required no reversal. The premise test was applied as well as the conclusion test: the donor does not reason from anything the 2025 Act does, so there is no premature premise to remove.

TASK-BOUNDARY CHANGE, NOT A TEMPORAL ONE. The removal of the crew's medical certificate from the answer is driven by the printed words of this stem and not by any change in the law. MLC 2006 Standard A1.2 is unchanged between the sittings; it is simply not what this paper asks about. Recorded here so that a later reader does not mistake a scope decision for a currency decision.

subpart_marks_note: Expands the November wording: November asks "What are the different certificates in India"; December splits this into the certificates issued and who may issue them, and adds a printed (16) that November omits.
